Symptoms of chronic periodic earaches along with purulent exudate began about one week after the patient suffered a water skiing accident on a river in Australia. The condition lasted for three years, until his ear exudate was examined in a clinical laboratory, diagnosed and treated.

summary.text: A 27-year-old Caucasian man presented to an otolaryngologist in Haifa, Israel, after three years of periodic earache with malodorous purulent exudate from the right ear, without fever. Symptoms began about one week after a 2011 water skiing accident on the Murray River in Australia in which his right eardrum was perforated. Earlier ear cleansings and aspirations had not helped.

An ear swab of the exudate taken during admission grew prominent bacteria on three agar media. VITEK-2 and MALDI-TOF identified Vibrio cholerae, confirmed by ompW PCR, and the reference laboratory called it non-O1/O139 and cholera toxin-negative. All five isolates were serogroup O100, positive for hapA, hlyA, ompU and toxR, negative for ctxA and other tested virulence genes, resistant to polymyxin B and susceptible to five other antibiotics.

Based on the susceptibility results, ciprofloxacin ear drops were used until the symptoms disappeared completely. An additional right ear swab sent three weeks later was negative for V. cholerae. The authors state the patient had none of the complications of untreated otitis media.

ambiguities.issue: The case text calls the presentation "acute otitis media" while the abstract calls it "recurrent otitis media" (and "chronic periodic earaches"); symptoms lasted three years. These are course descriptors that are not mutually exclusive, not two values of one measurement, so this is an ambiguity, not a source conflict; the condition is recorded as plain otitis media.
